questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Swapping the Order of Integration
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/48d76f34becfba9f58658c3c38ba2df0e76ad6ff20b83ffc836e213c4eea4565.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx.$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[6]{\pi },\,\,{y}^{3}\le z\le \sqrt{\pi }}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/86af6e58f4f13e79bb9672cef329572f006e5f4875178ede7908bddbd0dec404.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/83041605fcd79db34f249664b12311a4e5d797c331bcaf1279f03b5b68891b23.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{z}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/b5a3fc034b713ce5fca98fbd0cca3c454d18e42e0e73eecc7ec18c51a8e7ebb5.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the bottom curve given by $z=\sqrt[3]{0}=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/54fa3b1c3a15391e0a87c15017b07594c4f2cca7fb741cd7480909a64e3d39db.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[6]{\pi }}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2}){[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\frac{1}{3}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}+{z}^{2})]}_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[x]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Swapping the Order of Integration
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/22058df7ac75e085e1dc352736d1abf289e80d68f340ee63687e69d18e9b23c2.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dx\,dy\,dz.$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dx\,dy\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le \pi ,\,\,0\le y\le \pi ,\,\,0\le x\le y}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/c5eec166cdce2fa4be756aa144b6a802082def0374c2b6150794cb2f0f22f1a6.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/50a93024f817970869a3dcef831abc2515fe14efac5ec9dd778701d063b8351d.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=y\,⟹\,y=x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=\pi .
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,x\le y\le \pi },
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/ec3bc5a58b5521286388294b97e1449bb41548004477d6d4555c9b7b917f2bd7.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the right curve given by $x=\pi .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/205c88cdd0b8a2676bc8396760095fa238ae39acd3660ed5aba2df3726161410.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\,0\le z\le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dx\,dy\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{x}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\,dy\,dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}[{\int }_{x}^{\pi }\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}[y]_{x}^{\pi }\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\pi -x}\cdot (\pi -x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[-\operatorname{cos}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-(-1-1)\,\text{d}z \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\text{d}z \\  & =2[z]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Change the order of integration in the integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{\sqrt{3}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $z,$ then $y,$ and then $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{\sqrt{3}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,\sqrt{z}\le y\le \sqrt{3}}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3}.
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/3771c3587542c781136e1802cf2ad809aaa7aff701328963572fe9296c1eb856.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $\sqrt{z}\le y\le \sqrt{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/8e2aeb803b0458864560f894c3ec8635c38ac4b9febeb172115f4b3216fc44a5.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/385eed97efeb951228a44009faf76dc676f565204885c8f0df2cee0afc1657a8.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y=\sqrt{z}\,⟺\,z={y}^{2}.
$$

- The bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le {y}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/837b43fa43b6d160d0734a629f08bb415bd91f382b99dbd6a5c227dd46b98f29.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xy$-plane with the top curve given by $y=\sqrt{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/90dc40b39cd7a3fdfcff0469b1915dcd64811a16aad0dad452c8f57d4118546b.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{3}}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $z,$ then $y,$ then $x,$ we obtain

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{3}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

questions.problem:
Change the order of integration in the integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{y}-1}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ and then $z.$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(y,z),$ ${u}_{2}(y,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{y}-1}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\,0\le x\le {e}^{y}-1}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type II region, we first sketch the projection onto the $yz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\,0\le z\le 2}.
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/61d029135038017b000de51c15d8b392c0b80e98c49e78c8c82dfa79d6232878.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $0\le x\le {e}^{y}-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/08a4f528a01415112e5b194617f0fc450a0a849060f08fe1959e0929ef366316.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/4cd2d122764f82a6c38a9d657dcc579d2b93e676266604e03188ac933710dab0.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x={e}^{y}-1\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡3.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/69b31f925d432360dc0796c3745782bacb6645bbabcf159f9049770c09359757.png)

We now consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the right curve given by 

$$
x={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-1=2.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/dafed2ddc7ae18a05ec4fe1d5768f9b0f12456e0d2cf2552e91382d686d65522.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ then $z,$ we obtain

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{y}-1}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$

questions.problem:
${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{z/x}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x=$

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,y),$ ${u}_{2}(x,y),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{z/x}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2},\,\,\frac{z}{x}\le y\le x}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type III region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2}}
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/2b4cc501b983d6786c2e27680955a7ffdba17ff139ad4d9bed4a268521d365d9.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $\frac{z}{x}\le y\le x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/5c02178f02f39fa2ce2b27c0c51f58f33d9f2e7e54621e079e5645730cb20e56.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type I region and its projection $D$ onto the $xy$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $z$-axis and in the direction of increasing $z,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/f4c313659ca62d8d595fda91f53be9b10c6f7fa1105475b7e833d7f0a2e8acbe.png)

The arrow enters the region through the bottom boundary and leaves through the top boundary:

- The bottom boundary of the region is

$$
z=0.
$$

- The top boundary of the region, written in the form $z=z(x,y),$ is

$$
y=\frac{z}{x}\,⟺\,z=xy.
$$

Therefore, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le xy},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/79c4044d76be693decc1125ec88b53c162a6f29b0e701e0125319955bbe02fa1.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xy$-plane with the top curve given by $y=x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093829/assets/e123941fc02ba0ff653feffd0cc9b3f778fcd1c01ad2656b658e98fbcbae8b98.png)

Hence,

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le x}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{z/x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}{\int }_{0}^{xy}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})[{\int }_{0}^{xy}\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}8\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})[z]_{0}^{xy}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}8xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[4x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4}){\int }_{0}^{x}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4}){[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{4})]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(1).\end{aligned}
$$
